strengths: The information-geometric framing is well motivated and clearly presented: modeling molecules as composite exponential-family distributions and defining probability paths along e-geodesics is a coherent and elegant alternative to decoupled Euclidean/discrete diffusion paths.

The analysis of the Dirac-endpoint singularity (Appendix B, Fig. 2) and the demonstration that SLDM (Ni et al., 2025) is a special zero-curvature case of EGF under regularized boundary conditions (Appendix D) are genuine theoretical contributions that situate the method within the flow-matching literature.

Empirical results are strong and broad: near-reference PB-Valid (93.4%), dramatically better strain energy than all baselines (quartiles of 8.94/25.96/56.65 vs. hundreds for baselines), best Vina Dock, and consistent gains on MolGenBench scaffold metrics (Pass Rate 31.79%, Hit Recovery 72 targets) on both seen and unseen targets.

Ablations are substantive and cover the key design choices (evolving endpoint vs. static Dirac, Dirichlet parameterization, smoothing coefficient, explicit bond generation), and the loss-curve analysis in Appendix E convincingly illustrates the ill-conditioning of static EGF objectives.

The paper is honest about remaining limitations: absolute scaffold hit rates remain low across all methods and MolGenBench hit recovery drops to zero for out-of-distribution targets, with a reasonable discussion of what this implies for the field.

Implementation details (Algorithms 1-2, full hyperparameters, loss derivations in Appendix G, proof of equivalence to Fisher Flow Matching in Appendix F.3) support reproducibility of the described procedure.
weaknesses: The attribution of gains to the proposed geometric machinery is not fully isolated. The base architecture (unitransformer with edge, gated attention) is taken from MolPilot (Qiu et al., 2025), yet MolPilot is absent from the baseline tables despite sharing the same backbone and being a recent strong method. Without this comparison, it is unclear how much of the improvement comes from the EvoEGF path versus the network or explicit bond modeling.

The headline claim of alleviating 'modality mismatch' / enabling 'coupled contraction' is asserted rather than directly tested. The ablations compare evolving vs. static Dirac endpoints and different Dirichlet schedules, but there is no experiment isolating the e-geodesic path against a plain linear parameter-interpolation path (i.e., BFN/PIF-style) within the identical architecture. Given that the framework explicitly builds on BFN and PIF with 'linear interpolation replaced by an evolving exponential geodesic,' this is the pivotal ablation.

The practical algorithm is essentially parameter-space interpolation with hand-crafted schedules (σ1(t)=0.2(1−t)+ε; α1(t) with smoothing coefficient 0.2). The information-geometric interpretation, the induced velocity field (Eq. 9 with pseudoinverse), and the Fisher Flow Matching equivalence (Appendix F.3) are not actually exercised by the implementation, which risks the geometry being more narrative than functional. Theorem 1 (product of exponential families is exponential family) is trivial and does not establish the claimed cross-modal coupling beyond sharing a network.

Several results warrant more scrutiny: the ~10x improvement in strain energy over all baselines is striking and the paper does not disentangle how much is due to explicit bond diffusion vs. the flow construction; the smoothing coefficient and variance schedule appear to be sensitive hyperparameters found empirically (sweet spot at 0.2), with no guidance on how to set them for new domains.
No code release is mentioned, which limits reproducibility for a method whose performance depends on specific schedules and architectural details.

Writing has noticeable polish issues (e.g., 'a efficient strategy,' 'The metrics is shown'), and Section 3 refers readers to 'Sec.B' for the singularity analysis before the main text ever introduces it, slightly disrupting the flow. Minor metric inconsistencies (e.g., scaffold hit fraction stated as 1.08%/0.93% in text vs. table format) require care from the reader.

Baselines are evaluated on samples 'released from Qu et al. (2024)' and Cao et al. (2025) rather than re-run, which is standard but means protocol differences (e.g., sampling budgets, 100 vs. 1000 samples per target) are not controlled across methods.

strengths: The paper is clearly written and well organized, with a motivated information-geometric narrative (e-geodesics on Fisher-Rao manifolds) for unifying continuous coordinates and discrete atom/bond types in SBDD.

The analysis of the Dirac-endpoint singularity (Appendix B) and the demonstration that SLDM arises as a special, statically regularized case of EGF (Appendix D) are interesting observations that connect several recent methods.

The empirical evaluation is broad: CrossDocked2020 with PoseBusters/Vina/strain-energy metrics, MolGenBench real-world scaffold metrics, detailed ablations (Table 4), full PoseBusters breakdown (Table 5), and substructure distribution fidelity analyses (Tables 6-8, Figs 9-11).

The paper is commendably honest about absolute limitations, e.g., that scaffold hit rates remain below 5% and that hit recovery drops to zero for proteins outside the training distribution (Sec. H.1.2).
Training and sampling algorithms (Algorithms 1-2) are given explicitly, which aids reproducibility of the procedure.
weaknesses: The gap between theory and method is significant. The actual algorithm reduces to a hand-crafted schedule: sigma_1(t) = 0.2(1-t)+epsilon and a smoothed one-hot Dirichlet target (Algorithm 1, lines 3, 8-11). The elaborate Fisher-Rao/'pursuit-evasion' framing is not formalized; a path eta_t = (1-t)eta_0 + t*eta_1(t) with time-varying eta_1 is generally not a geodesic, so claims of geometric 'consistency with the Fisher-Rao information geometry' are not rigorously supported. In practice this is close to a reparameterized BFN/PIF with a modified noise schedule, which limits the claimed novelty.

The velocity-field construction (Eq. 9, Appendix F.2) is heuristic: it asserts a statistic-transport solution 'using the property that...' and introduces an unspecified scaling matrix C_t, rather than deriving a unique or verified solution to the continuity equation. The Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse formulation is not validated.

Central empirical claims lack statistical support: no seeds, repetitions, variance or confidence intervals are reported for any benchmark; baselines are evaluated on released samples from prior work rather than re-run under matched conditions, weakening the comparison.

Several methods discussed as context (FLOWR, ECloudGen, DynamicFlow, MolPilot, SLDM) are not included in the comparisons, even though MolPilot/SLDM directly address the same schedule-alignment problem the paper targets. The headline PB-Valid of 93.4% ('approaches reference level') is achieved against a somewhat dated baseline set; on Vina Score/Min the model is second to MolCRAFT.

The connection to Fisher Flow Matching (Appendix F.3) is essentially the standard local KL-to-squared-distance Taylor argument, and the resulting practical loss (weighted MSE, Eq. 10) is a diffusion-style objective; the framing overstates how different the training objective is from existing BFN/parameter-interpolation approaches.
Efficiency claims ('efficient training and sampling') are asserted but never measured: no wall-clock time, NFE, or memory comparisons against baselines are provided.

The 'optimal' hyperparameters (smoothing coefficient 0.2, sigma_1(t) slope 0.2) appear selected empirically on the test benchmark: Table 4 shows e.g. smooth coefficient 0.4 attains better Vina metrics while 0.2 attains better PB-Valid, and the selection criterion for 'Best' is not stated, raising concerns about test-set tuning.

Presentation issues: inconsistent section references (Sec. B referenced before Sec. 3.2 while the main text says 'Sec.3.2'), minor grammatical errors ('a efficient strategy', 'The metrics is shown'), and the 'highlights remaining limitations' subsection mixes benchmark description with conclusions.

No discussion of compute footprint, code release, or limitations section in the main text; the reproducibility picture is incomplete despite the pseudocode (no dataset splits beyond standard, no number of evaluation repeats, no sampling-cost analysis).

strengths: The core idea is well-motivated: treating continuous coordinates and discrete atom/bond types within a single composite exponential-family distribution and constructing probability paths along e-geodesics gives a principled geometric framing, and the identified failure mode of static Dirac endpoints (natural parameter divergence, variance collapse, 'support vanishing' in the Dirichlet case, Appendix B) is clearly articulated and convincingly demonstrated (Fig. 2, Fig. 8).

The evolving-endpoint strategy is well supported by ablations: the naive fixed-Dirac e-geodesic baseline fails catastrophically (PB-Valid 64.1%, positive Vina scores), and variants on Dirichlet parameterization, smoothing coefficient, and bond diffusion are all individually analyzed (Table 4, Appendix H.2), which substantiates the central design claim.

The theoretical appendix is a genuine asset: the derivation showing SLDM (Ni et al., 2025) is a regularized zero-curvature special case of EGF (Appendix D), the equivalence between the local transport objective and Fisher flow matching (Appendix F.3), and the loss derivations (Appendix G) connect the method to existing literature rigorously.

Experiments are broad and multi-angle: CrossDocked2020 with PoseBusters, Vina variants, strain energy, and substructure distributions (Tables 1, 5-8), plus the real-world-oriented MolGenBench scaffold metrics (Table 2). The strain-energy improvement (quartiles of ~9/26/57 vs. hundreds-thousands for baselines) and near-reference bond length/angle distributions (Fig. 4, 9-11) are compelling evidence of geometric fidelity.

The paper is honest about limitations: it explicitly acknowledges that absolute scaffold hit rates remain below 5% and that hit recovery drops to zero on unseen targets, framing these as open gaps rather than hiding them.
weaknesses: The 'unified statistical manifold' claim is weaker than presented. The composite distribution is a product of per-atom/per-edge exponential families (Theorem 1 is essentially trivial closure of exponential families under products), so continuous and discrete modalities are still modeled independently at the path level. The claimed 'coupled contraction' of identity and geometry arises from the network architecture, not from the geometric construction itself; the framing risks overselling what the e-geodesic path actually contributes over a BFN/PIF-style scheme with a tuned variance schedule.

The abstract and introduction conflate terminology: e-geodesics are geodesics under the exponential (e-) connection and are flat in natural parameters; they are not geodesics 'under the Fisher-Rao metric.' This imprecision recurs and should be corrected.

The induced sample-space velocity field (Eq. 9, 22) with the pseudoinverse and an unspecified scaling matrix Ct described as locally 'optimal' is underdeveloped, and it is unclear whether this field is actually used in training or sampling — Algorithm 1/2 operate purely on parameter-space updates, leaving a gap between the geometric theory and the implemented method.

Baseline comparison is not fully up to date or self-contained: baselines are evaluated on released samples from prior papers (Qu et al., 2024; Cao et al., 2025), and several cited recent methods with strong reported results (FLOWR, MolPilot, ECloudGen) are discussed but not compared. No significance tests or variance over multiple seeds are reported, and computational/sampling cost relative to baselines is absent.

The evolving target introduces hand-tuned hyperparameters (sigma_1(t) = lambda(1-t), smoothing coefficient 0.2, chosen via a sweet-spot analysis) that slightly undercut the 'principled geometry' narrative; the method reduces in practice to a progressive-parameter-refinement model with a particular schedule, and the paper should be more explicit about this.

Reproducibility is limited: no code release or supplementary artifact is mentioned, and key implementation choices (16-hour training, batch size 16, kNN 32) are given but cannot currently be verified; the pass-rate of 93.4% and MolGenBench gains are therefore difficult for others to independently confirm.

strengths: The paper presents a coherent information-geometric framework (evolving e-geodesics in natural-parameter space) that unifies continuous coordinates (Gaussian) and discrete types (Dirichlet) for SBDD, with a clearly explained motivation: static Dirac endpoints cause premature variance/concentration collapse on the statistical manifold.

The theoretical contributions are non-trivial and well-documented: the singularity analysis of Dirac targets (Appendix B), the proof that dynamic endpoints cannot be reduced to non-linear time reparameterization of a fixed endpoint (Appendix D), the derivation of SLDM as a regularized special case of EGF (Appendix E), and the local Fisher-Rao interpretation of the KL objective (Appendices H.2, H.3).

Empirical evaluation is comprehensive: strong PoseBusters validity (93.4%) on CrossDock approaching the reference data (95.0%), large improvements in strain energy (8.94/25.96/56.65 quartiles vs. 83-13871 for baselines), strong MolGenBench scaffold metrics, detailed PoseBusters sub-test breakdowns, intermediate-state analysis, and distribution-matching figures for bond lengths/angles/torsions.

Ablation studies (Table 4, Appendix J.2) directly support the central design claim: the naive fixed-Dirac EGF baseline fails catastrophically (64.1% PB-Valid, positive Vina score), while the evolving endpoint, Dirichlet parameterization, smoothing coefficient, and explicit bond modeling each contribute measurably.

Reproducibility support is good: full training and sampling algorithms with concrete hyperparameters and schedules, architecture and compute details, and derivations of all losses. The limitations are discussed honestly (low absolute scaffold hit rates <5%, zero hit recovery on unseen targets, drug-likeness caveats in the case study), and an impact statement is included.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate rather than fundamental: the generative procedure is explicitly a BFN/PIF-style progressive-parameter-refinement model (MolCRAFT, MolPIF already occupy this design space for SBDD), and the key new ingredient reduces to a specific variance/concentration schedule σ̃1(t)=λ(1−t) and α̃1(t) mixing toward a uniform vector. The Fisher-Rao framing is largely motivational, since training operates on a one-step KL with only a local (second-order) Fisher-Rao interpretation rather than actual geodesic optimization on the manifold.

Missing direct comparison with the strongest SOTA baseline in the main results: MolPilot (Qiu et al., 2025), which supplies the released samples used for evaluation and reportedly achieves a slightly higher PB-Valid than EvoEGF-Mol (acknowledged only in Appendix F). A head-to-head in Tables 1-2 would materially strengthen the empirical claims.

The abstract claims 'approaches a reference-level PoseBusters passing rate (93.4%)' on CrossDock, but the reported reference is 95.0%, and Vina Score (-6.14) and several other metrics are second to MolCRAFT; the overall superiority claim ('significantly outperforms traditional SBDD generative models across multiple benchmarks') is more nuanced than the headline suggests.

No statistical uncertainty is reported (no error bars, seeds, or significance tests) for the main benchmarks; the very large strain-energy advantage (8.94 vs. 83 for the next best) is surprising and, while the authors state a common evaluation pipeline, would benefit from verification or explanation (e.g., sensitivity to minimization protocol).

Presentation flaws reduce polish: the code URL in the abstract is empty ('Code is available at'), there are typographical artifacts (e.g., 'PB-Valid score substantially surpasses those' immediately followed by contradictory phrasing, figure typos such as 'Comformation'), and the motivating 'modality mismatch' argument would benefit from a direct empirical demonstration rather than citation of prior work.

Some methodological choices are under-justified: using a Dirichlet distribution as the sample-space object for categorical variables (rather than flows directly on the simplex) is unusual, and the sensitivity of results to the single smoothing coefficient λ=0.2 (performance drops noticeably at 0.1) suggests the framework requires nontrivial schedule tuning despite claims of principled design.

strengths: The paper offers a coherent information-geometric formulation: representing molecules as products of exponential-family distributions and constructing probability paths as linear interpolations in natural parameter space (e-geodesics) provides a principled alternative to separately designed Euclidean/categorical schedules (Secs. 3.1-3.2).

The theoretical analysis is more than decorative: Appendix D proves that dynamic endpoints are not reducible to non-linear time reparameterizations of fixed-endpoint paths (Eq. 16-17), and Appendix E derives SLDM as a special case of EGF under shared boundary noise, which situates the contribution relative to recent work (Ni et al., 2025). The local Fisher-Rao interpretation of the KL objective (Appendix H.3) is a nice touch.

The empirical evaluation is broad: CrossDock (Table 1), a real-world-oriented MolGenBench scaffold benchmark (Table 2), full PoseBusters breakdowns (Table 5), substructure distribution matching (Tables 8-10), intermediate-state analysis (Tables 6-7), and ablations covering the evolving strategy, Dirichlet parameterization, smoothing coefficient, bond generation, and sampling steps (Table 4). The ablation on the naive static Dirac EGF (PB-Valid 64.1%, positive Vina) directly supports the central claim about endpoint singularity.

Honest limitations discussion: the paper explicitly acknowledges that absolute scaffold hit rates remain low (<5%) and that geometric plausibility alone cannot bridge the drug-discovery efficiency gap, and Appendix J.1 reports zero hit recovery for unseen targets.
Reproducibility assets are present: full training and sampling pseudocode (Algorithms 1-2), architecture/optimizer details, runtime, and derived loss functions (Appendix I).
weaknesses: The central 'unified manifold' framing is partially rhetorical. Under the product assumption the Fisher matrix is block diagonal (Eq. 11), so the modalities remain statistically independent; synchronization is achieved not by geometry but by a hand-crafted smoothing coefficient λ=0.2 in σ̃1(t) and α̃1(t), which is tuned via a sweep (Appendix J.2). This reintroduces exactly the kind of heuristic weighting the paper claims to avoid ('automatically calibrated by the intrinsic uncertainty... rather than relying on heuristically designed weights').

The strongest and most relevant baseline, MolPilot (Qiu et al., 2025), is excluded from the main tables and only discussed in Appendix F, where the authors concede EvoEGF-Mol achieves a lower PB-Valid. Given that MolPilot directly targets the same modality-schedule mismatch problem, its omission from Tables 1-2 weakens the 'significantly outperforms baselines' claim; on CrossDock the Vina Score advantage over MolCRAFT is also marginal (-6.14 vs -6.55 avg).

Novelty over the BFN/PIF paradigm (Graves et al., 2023; Jin et al., 2025) is incremental: the generative machinery is explicitly 'inspired by' and 'follows' these frameworks, and the actual implementation reduces to Gaussian/Dirichlet natural-parameter interpolation with a parametric decay schedule — e-geodesics for Gaussians are classical. The contribution is essentially a schedule redesign plus theoretical packaging.

No statistical rigor: results appear to come from single runs with no seed variance, confidence intervals, or significance tests, despite differences between methods that are often small (e.g., SA, QED, Clash Ratio in Tables 1 and 4).

Reproducibility gaps: the abstract states 'Code is available at' with no URL provided, and several ablation configurations (e.g., the exact Dirichlet smoothing vector variants) lack full hyperparameter disclosure.

Some empirical claims are loosely supported: 'approaches a reference-level PoseBusters passing rate (93.4%)' is actually below the CrossDock reference (95.0%) and below MolPilot per the authors' own appendix; the improvement narrative in Sec. 4.2 ('substantially surpasses those of other baselines') should be tempered by the missing top baseline comparison.

Writing issues: 'the result of molecule is sampled at t=1' (Sec. 3.3), 'The metrics is shown in Table 1', and 'Comformation Stability' (Appendix J.5) indicate insufficient proofreading for a camera-ready-quality submission.

strengths: The paper offers a principled information-geometric formulation: representing coordinates, atom types, and bond types as product exponential-family distributions and interpolating along e-geodesics in natural-parameter space gives a unified probability path for mixed continuous/discrete molecular generation, with a Fisher-Rao-grounded KL training objective (Eqs. 11, 12, 13).

The dynamic-endpoint (EvoEGF) idea is well motivated: the analysis of Dirac-target singularity (Appendix B, Fig. 2, Fig. 7, Fig. 8) convincingly explains why static e-geodesic endpoints cause premature variance/concentration collapse, and the ablation showing the naïve fixed-Dirac EGF fails catastrophically (PB-Valid 64.1%, positive Vina score) directly supports the core design choice.

The connection to SLDM as a special case of EGF under regularized boundary conditions (Appendix E) and the proof that dynamic endpoints are not reducible to non-linear time reparameterization (Appendix D) add genuine conceptual value and situate the method relative to prior work.

Empirical results are strong and broad: near-reference PB-Valid (93.4%) on CrossDock, dramatically lower strain-energy quartiles (8.94/25.96/56.65 vs. 83–13871 for baselines), best atom-type/ring/functional-group distribution match (Tables 8–10), earlier emergence of valid molecular prototypes during sampling (Table 6), and consistent gains over baselines on the real-world MolGenBench scaffold metrics (Table 2).

Reproducibility is good: full training/sampling algorithms with explicit schedules and hyperparameters (Algorithms 1–2), implementation details, and released code are provided; robustness to reduced sampling steps (n=20, 50) is also reported.
The limitations are discussed honestly, e.g., the admission that absolute scaffold hit rates remain low (<5%) and that geometric plausibility alone does not bridge the gap to bioactivity.
weaknesses: Incremental theoretical novelty relative to known tools: e-geodesics as linear natural-parameter interpolation is classical information geometry, and the 'evolving endpoint' amounts in practice to a hand-designed variance/concentration schedule (σ̃1(t)=λ(1−t), λ=0.2 tuned empirically). The Fisher-calibrated loss weighting claim is weakened by the fact that modality losses are simply summed and the smoothing coefficient still requires per-framework tuning.

Baseline coverage and fairness: Table 1 omits the strongest recent competitors — MolPilot is acknowledged in Appendix F to achieve a higher PB-Valid score than EvoEGF-Mol, yet is excluded from the main comparison; FLOWR and other recent flow-based SBDD models are also not directly compared. All baseline numbers come from released samples of prior papers rather than a unified re-run, which complicates exact comparability.

No statistical rigor for the headline claims: results are reported without error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests. The extreme strain-energy improvement (an order of magnitude over all baselines) is striking but unverified and not cross-validated with an independent metric pipeline; the possibility of hyperparameter overfitting to the CrossDock test set (λ, σ1, α schedules selected by test-metric ablations in Table 4) is not addressed.

Some central claims are asserted rather than demonstrated: e.g., that synchronized natural-parameter evolution 'mitigates the temporal-scale mismatch' is supported mostly by indirect evidence (intermediate-state validity), and the Fisher-Rao tangent machinery (Eqs. 8–10) is not actually used in the training objective beyond a second-order KL approximation.

Presentation issues: the abstract's code URL is broken/truncated ('Code is available at' with no link); several grammatical errors ('The metrics is shown'), a typo in Figure 1 caption ('Samp le'), and the O(N²) Dirichlet bond modeling raises a computational cost concern that is only briefly discussed (1.5 mol/s on an RTX 4090) without a compute comparison table against baselines.

The practical benefit over closely related methods (MolCRAFT's BFN, MolPilot's optimized schedules, SLDM's regularized endpoints) reduces to a specific schedule choice; the paper would be strengthened by a direct head-to-head against MolPilot under identical training data and architecture.
